plan.question: Are soccer referees more likely to give red cards to dark-skin-toned players than to light-skin-toned players?

steps.title: Handle players without skin-tone ratings
steps.description: Skin tone is only available for players who were rated from photos; the choice is whether to keep only rated rows (required for the exposure) and whether to additionally require the other covariates used later.

options.label: Keep rows with both rater scores
options.rationale: Rows with a missing exposure cannot enter the comparison; this is the minimal requirement.
options.spec: Drop rows where rater1 or rater2 is missing (use the rows where both rater1 and rater2 are non-null). Create no new columns and write nothing to ctx. Return the filtered data frame.

options.label: Keep rated rows with complete position, height and weight
options.rationale: Restricts to rows where all candidate covariates are observed so every model is fit on the same sample.
options.spec: Drop rows where rater1, rater2, position, height or weight is missing. Create no new columns and write nothing to ctx. Return the filtered data frame.

steps.title: Construct the skin-tone exposure
steps.description: Build a binary dark-vs-light exposure from the two raters' scores; the cut-off and rater combination are alternatives.

options.label: Average of raters, split at median
options.rationale: Uses both raters and a data-driven split, common in this literature.
options.spec: Compute skin_mean = (rater1 + rater2) / 2 per row. Compute the median of skin_mean over rows that have it. Set dark_skin = 1 where skin_mean is strictly greater than that median, else 0; write the median to ctx['skin_cut'] as a number. Return the data frame.

options.label: Average of raters, split at scale midpoint
options.rationale: A fixed cut at the middle of the 0 to 1 scale avoids a data-dependent threshold.
options.spec: Compute skin_mean = (rater1 + rater2) / 2 per row. Set dark_skin = 1 where skin_mean is strictly greater than 0.5, else 0 (rows with missing skin_mean stay missing). Write 0.5 to ctx['skin_cut']. Return the data frame.

options.label: Rater 1 only, split at median
options.rationale: Uses a single rater, giving a check on inter-rater dependence of the result.
options.spec: Set dark_skin = 1 where rater1 is strictly greater than the median of rater1 over rows that have it, else 0 (missing stays missing). Write that median to ctx['skin_cut']. Also create skin_mean = rater1 so the column exists. Return the data frame.

steps.title: Treatment of extreme referee-country bias scores and extreme games
steps.description: meanIAT, meanExp and games have extreme values; whether to keep them, trim the referee-country score or cap exposure days is a visible choice.

options.label: Keep all rows
options.rationale: Extreme values are genuine observations in these columns; no trimming.
options.spec: Do not remove any rows. Create no new columns and write nothing to ctx. Return the data frame unchanged.

options.label: Drop rows with extreme meanIAT or meanExp
options.rationale: Referee-country bias scores far from the bulk may reflect very small country samples.
options.spec: Drop rows where meanIAT lies outside the 1st to 99th percentile range of meanIAT or meanExp lies outside the 1st to 99th percentile range of meanExp (compute the percentiles over non-missing values). Create no new columns and write nothing to ctx. Return the filtered data frame.

options.label: Keep rows with games at most 20
options.rationale: Very long dyads dominate the count outcome; restricting to a plausible range tests sensitivity to them.
options.spec: Drop rows where games is greater than 20. Create no new columns and write nothing to ctx. Return the filtered data frame.

steps.title: Estimate the odds ratio of a red card by skin tone
steps.description: Alternative logistic estimators of the odds ratio of a red card for dark vs light skin tone, using the covariates in ctx['covariates']; the outcome is recorded as any red card or as a count per game.

options.label: Logistic regression on any red card, cluster-robust errors by player
options.rationale: Matches the stated odds-ratio metric directly by modelling whether a dyad produced any red card; clustering by player accounts for repeated rows.
options.spec: Create any_red = 1 where redCards is greater than 0, else 0. Fit statsmodels Logit with outcome any_red, regressors dark_skin plus the columns in ctx['covariates'] (categorical ones encoded with drop_first=True) and an intercept, using cov_type='cluster' with groups = playerShort codes. Estimate = exp(coefficient of dark_skin); ci_low and ci_high = exp of the 95% Wald interval bounds; p_value = two-sided p for dark_skin. Return these four numbers.

options.label: Logistic regression on any red card, heteroskedasticity-robust errors
options.rationale: Gives the same odds-ratio scale with ordinary robust errors, a check on whether clustering by player changes the interval.
options.spec: Create any_red = 1 where redCards is greater than 0, else 0. Fit statsmodels Logit with outcome any_red, regressors dark_skin plus the columns in ctx['covariates'] (categorical ones encoded with drop_first=True) and an intercept, using cov_type='HC1'. Estimate = exp(coefficient of dark_skin); ci_low and ci_high = exp of the 95% Wald interval bounds; p_value = two-sided p for dark_skin. Return these four numbers.

options.label: Logistic regression on red cards per game, cluster-robust errors by player
options.rationale: Uses the count of red cards with games as the trial count through a binomial model, so the odds ratio refers to a red card per game, as the metric states.
options.spec: Create red_per_game = redCards / games. Fit statsmodels GLM with family Binomial and logit link on red_per_game with var_weights = games (frequency weights of games), regressors dark_skin plus the columns in ctx['covariates'] (categorical ones encoded with drop_first=True) and an intercept, using cov_type='cluster' with groups = playerShort codes. Estimate = exp(coefficient of dark_skin); ci_low and ci_high = exp of the 95% Wald interval bounds; p_value = two-sided p for dark_skin. Return these four numbers.

data.reason: Keeping all rows is the standard practice for this step: the column notes describe meanIAT, meanExp and games as genuine observations, and no outlier rule is pre-specified. Retaining every dyad preserves the estimand and avoids outcome-driven trimming.

Dropping dyads with games above 20 removes genuine data on the exposure-outcome relation in a count outcome; the rationale (long dyads dominate the count) is a weak, sensitivity-style reason and the cut-off of 20 has no field basis since games is a shared-game count per dyad, so it is questionable and needs strong special justification rather than a plausible-range rule.

Requiring position, height and weight to be observed shrinks the sample to rows with complete covariates, which is a reasonable choice only if those covariates enter the model. The rationale is about model comparability, not about the exposure. The conventional option already yields the estimand; this extra complete-case restriction drops rows for reasons unrelated to the exposure and is defensible only with a stated need for a common sample. It is questionable rather than standard, so it falls below the acceptance threshold.

Rater 1 alone is a valid sensitivity check on measurement, but the column notes say rater1 takes many values (it is a 0-to-1 score), and the spec splits it at its own median, which is a reasonable operationalisation. However, the rationale is only that it gives a check on inter-rater dependence, and a single rater's idiosyncratic scoring is a weaker proxy for skin tone than the average of both raters; the option is a questionable alternative needing stronger justification. The spec itself is coherent (missing stays missing, cut written to ctx), so the concern is construct validity rather than mechanics.

Restricting to dyad rows with both skin-tone ratings is the required minimal exposure filter; the rated rows are the only ones where the exposure exists, and no new columns or outcome-based choices are introduced. Rows lacking photo ratings are plausibly different, but this is the standard handling and it is a defensible, conventional choice given the estimand.

Trimming the referee-country bias scores at the 1st and 99th percentiles is a defensible sensitivity check on a country-level covariate, but meanIAT and meanExp are country-level scores shared by many dyads, so trimming removes whole countries and a large set of rows without a data-quality justification. The rationale (small country samples) is plausible but the cut-off is arbitrary and the filter is not a standard practice for this estimand; it reads as a questionable choice needing strong special justification, and it does not address the stated extreme games variable.

Averaging the two independent raters' skin-tone scores and splitting at the median is the standard, defensible way to build a binary dark-vs-light exposure from this data; it uses both raters, keeps the comparison within the question, and the median cut is a data-driven, non-outcome-driven choice. Both raters take five distinct values on 0-1 scale, consistent with the column notes.

Averaging the two raters and splitting at the fixed scale midpoint is a legitimate alternative operationalisation of dark versus light skin tone that avoids a data-dependent median threshold; it changes which rows fall in which group, which is the sensitivity being studied, but it still measures the same construct. Its defensibility is moderate because the scale midpoint is a conventional but not obviously meaningful cut for a skin-tone rating, and the rater values take only five distinct levels so the split may be close to the median anyway.

The question asks whether referees treat dark- and light-skinned players differently, which is a comparison at equal values of other factors. Position, league country and referee country are plausible pre-exposure confounders (they shape both player skin tone composition and card rates), so leaving them out keeps that confounding in the estimate. The unadjusted comparison is a crude association that does not answer the question.

Player position, league country and referee country are plausible pre-exposure drivers of card rates and are measured before the rating-based exposure, so adjusting for them estimates the association at comparable roles and contexts without confounding by league or referee nationality. This is the conventional and standard covariate set for this question, consistent with the published analysis of this dataset (Gaddis/Parsons-style adjusted models).

Adding player height and weight (pre-exposure, player characteristics that may plausibly relate to disciplinary outcomes) and referee-country bias scores (pre-exposure, plausibly linked to both referee attitudes and rater skin tone perception) is a reasonable confounder-control alternative for an observational estimand about what skin tone does. Games is the number of shared games, which is an exposure-scaling variable a reviewer would accept with justification, though it is closer to an offset than a confounder. The set is a genuine change from the conventional spec and does not reverse direction or leak the outcome.

Heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) errors on the same logit with the same odds-ratio estimand is a standard, defensible alternative to clustering when the observations are treated as independent. It is a different variance estimator rather than a rescaling or a no-op, but it ignores player-level repetition (many dyad rows per player), so its intervals are likely too narrow; the conventional player-clustered option is the more appropriate one here, which keeps this near but below the top of the range.

Modelling red cards per game with a binomial GLM using games as frequency weights is a legitimate way to target a per-game rate, but it changes the outcome from any red card (the conventional option) to a count-based proportion and gives 2,053 clusters with redCards taking only 3 distinct values. Frequency weights with a fractional outcome are unusual and not standard for a logit of an event indicator; the rationale merely restates the metric rather than justifying a different estimand, so it is questionable but not clearly defensible.

Logistic regression on any red card per dyad with cluster-robust errors by player (2,053 clusters, well above 30) is a standard, defensible way to estimate an odds ratio for red card by skin tone, and the dyad rows repeat players so clustering is appropriate. The main weakness is that the 'any red card' outcome discards the count information and dark_skin is a dichotomised rater skin tone, but this is a reasonable operationalisation the field uses.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def apply(df, ctx):
    out = df.copy()
    out["skin_mean"] = (out["rater1"] + out["rater2"]) / 2.0
    med = float(np.nanmedian(out["skin_mean"].to_numpy(dtype=float)))
    ctx["skin_cut"] = med
    dark = (out["skin_mean"] > med).astype(float)
    dark = dark.where(out["skin_mean"].notna(), float("nan"))
    out["dark_skin"] = dark
    return out

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def apply(df, ctx):
    out = df.copy()
    out["skin_mean"] = (out["rater1"] + out["rater2"]) / 2.0
    out["dark_skin"] = (out["skin_mean"] > 0.5).astype(float)
    out.loc[out["skin_mean"].isna(), "dark_skin"] = float("nan")
    ctx["skin_cut"] = 0.5
    return out

Fit statsmodels Logit with outcome any_red, regressors dark_skin plus the columns in ctx['covariates'] (categorical ones encoded with drop_first=True) and an intercept, using cov_type='cluster' with groups = playerShort codes. Estimate = exp(coefficient of dark_skin); ci_low and ci_high = exp of the 95% Wald interval bounds; p_value = two-sided p for dark_skin. Return these four numbers.
options.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm

def estimate(df, ctx):
    covs = list(ctx["covariates"])
    cols = ["redCards", "dark_skin", "playerShort"] + covs
    data = df.dropna(subset=cols).copy()
    data["any_red"] = (data["redCards"] > 0).astype(float)
    X = data[["dark_skin"] + covs].copy()
    cat_cols = [c for c in covs if not pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(X[c])]
    X = pd.get_dummies(X, columns=cat_cols, drop_first=True, dtype=float)
    X = X.astype(float)
    X.insert(0, "const", 1.0)
    groups = pd.factorize(data["playerShort"])[0]
    y = data["any_red"].astype(float)
    model = sm.Logit(y, X)
    fit = model.fit(disp=0, cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": groups})
    i = list(X.columns).index("dark_skin")
    beta = float(fit.params.iloc[i]) if hasattr(fit.params, "iloc") else float(fit.params[i])
    ci = np.asarray(fit.conf_int())[i]
    pv = float(np.asarray(fit.pvalues)[i])
    return {
        "estimate": float(np.exp(beta)),
        "ci_low": float(np.exp(ci[0])),
        "ci_high": float(np.exp(ci[1])),
        "p_value": pv,
        "n": int(len(data)),
    }

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm

def estimate(df, ctx):
    data = df.copy()
    data["any_red"] = (data["redCards"] > 0).astype(float)
    covariates = list(ctx["covariates"])
    cols = ["any_red", "dark_skin"] + covariates
    data = data.dropna(subset=cols)
    cat_cols = [c for c in covariates if not pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[c])]
    num_cols = [c for c in covariates if c not in cat_cols]
    X = pd.get_dummies(data[cat_cols], drop_first=True, dtype=float) if cat_cols else pd.DataFrame(index=data.index)
    X = pd.concat([data[["dark_skin"] + num_cols].astype(float), X], axis=1)
    for c in num_cols:
        if c != "dark_skin" and X[c].std() > 0:
            X[c] = (X[c] - X[c].mean()) / X[c].std()
    X = sm.add_constant(X, has_constant="add")
    model = sm.Logit(data["any_red"].astype(float).values, X.astype(float).values)
    fit = model.fit(disp=0, cov_type="HC1")
    i = list(X.columns).index("dark_skin")
    beta = fit.params[i]
    lo, hi = fit.conf_int()[i]
    return {
        "estimate": float(np.exp(beta)),
        "ci_low": float(np.exp(lo)),
        "ci_high": float(np.exp(hi)),
        "p_value": float(fit.pvalues[i]),
        "n": int(len(data)),
    }

option.label: Average of raters, dark = top quartile vs bottom quartile
option.rationale: Skin tone is a continuous rating with rater disagreement; comparing only the extremes of the rating distribution is a standard way to contrast clearly dark with clearly light players and reduces misclassification near the middle of the scale, a common practice in skin-tone discrimination studies.
option.spec: Compute skin_mean = (rater1 + rater2) / 2 per row. Compute the 25th and 75th percentiles of skin_mean over rows that have it. Set dark_skin = 1 where skin_mean is at or above the 75th percentile, dark_skin = 0 where skin_mean is at or below the 25th percentile, and dark_skin = missing for rows in between (exclude them). Write the 75th percentile to ctx['skin_cut'] as a number. Return the data frame.

option.label: Position, league, referee country plus player and game-exposure covariates
option.rationale: Player height, weight and the number of shared games are plausible determinants of card counts per dyad and are recorded per row, so adjusting for them is defensible without using outcome information; referee-country bias scores are excluded here to avoid collinearity with the country fixed effects.
option.spec: Write ctx['covariates'] = ['position', 'leagueCountry', 'refCountry', 'height', 'weight', 'games']. Do not add or drop columns. Return the data frame. The model encodes categorical columns with drop_first=True.

option.label: Poisson rate model on red-card count with games exposure, clustered by player
option.rationale: Because the estimand is a rate per game and games varies by dyad, modelling the count of red cards with log(games) as an exposure offset matches the question's per-game framing better than a binary indicator, and clustering by player accounts for repeated dyads.
option.spec: Fit statsmodels GLM with outcome redCards, family Poisson (log link), regressors dark_skin plus the columns in ctx['covariates'] (categorical ones encoded with drop_first=True) and an intercept, with offset = log(games) (games must be >0; drop rows with games <= 0 first), using cov_type='cluster' with groups = playerShort codes. Estimate = exp(coefficient of dark_skin); ci_low and ci_high = exp of the 95% Wald interval bounds; p_value = two-sided p for dark_skin. Return these four numbers.

data.reason: Comparing only the extremes of the averaged skin-tone rating is a recognised sensitivity analysis and does not change the construct, but it discards the middle half of rows (about half the data) and the quartile cut-offs are not the field's standard split; with rater scores on only five distinct values, quartiles can tie heavily so the dark and light groups may be unequal or ill-defined. It is a questionable choice needing special justification rather than a standard or clearly reasonable alternative.

The estimand is a rate per game with games varying by dyad, so a Poisson model with log(games) offset matches the per-game framing, and clustering by player (2,053 clusters, repeated across dyads) is defensible. It is a reasonable alternative to the binary logit, though it models counts rather than the odds ratio asked for, so a sentence of justification is needed.

Height and weight are measured before the card decision and plausibly relate to playing style and card counts; games is the exposure of each dyad row (more shared games mechanically means more opportunity for cards), so adjusting for it is a sound offset-like control. Keeping position, league and referee country as in the conventional set, and excluding the referee-country bias scores, keeps the adjustment set pre-exposure and free of outcome leakage. The estimand (the odds of a red card per dyad game, dark vs light skin tone) is unchanged, and the added covariates are not a no-op since they alter the estimate.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def apply(df, ctx):
    out = df.copy()
    out["skin_mean"] = (out["rater1"] + out["rater2"]) / 2.0
    med = float(np.nanmedian(out["skin_mean"].to_numpy(dtype=float)))
    ctx["skin_cut"] = med
    dark = (out["skin_mean"] > med).astype(float)
    dark = dark.where(out["skin_mean"].notna(), float("nan"))
    out["dark_skin"] = dark
    return out

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def apply(df, ctx):
    out = df.copy()
    out["skin_mean"] = (out["rater1"] + out["rater2"]) / 2.0
    out["dark_skin"] = (out["skin_mean"] > 0.5).astype(float)
    out.loc[out["skin_mean"].isna(), "dark_skin"] = float("nan")
    ctx["skin_cut"] = 0.5

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm

def estimate(df, ctx):
    covs = list(ctx["covariates"])
    cols = ["redCards", "dark_skin", "playerShort"] + covs
    data = df.dropna(subset=cols).copy()
    data["any_red"] = (data["redCards"] > 0).astype(float)
    X = data[["dark_skin"] + covs].copy()
    cat_cols = [c for c in covs if not pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(X[c])]
    X = pd.get_dummies(X, columns=cat_cols, drop_first=True, dtype=float)
    X = X.astype(float)
    X.insert(0, "const", 1.0)
    groups = pd.factorize(data["playerShort"])[0]
    y = data["any_red"].astype(float)
    model = sm.Logit(y, X)
    fit = model.fit(disp=0, cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": groups})
    i = list(X.columns).index("dark_skin")
    beta = float(fit.params.iloc[i]) if hasattr(fit.params, "iloc") else float(fit.params[i])
    ci = np.asarray(fit.conf_int())[i]
    pv = float(np.asarray(fit.pvalues)[i])
    return {
        "estimate": float(np.exp(beta)),
        "ci_low": float(np.exp(ci[0])),
        "ci_high": float(np.exp(ci[1])),
        "p_value": pv,
        "n": int(len(data)),
    }

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm


def estimate(df, ctx):
    names = [] + [str(c) for c in ctx.get('covariates', [])]
    core_names = ['redCards', 'dark_skin']
    allowed = {*core_names, *('C',)}
    words = lambda c: {
        t
        for t in ''.join(h if h.isalnum() or h in '_' else ' ' for h in c).split()
        if not t.isdigit()
    }
    plain = lambda c: '**' not in c and all(
        h.isalnum() or h in '_ :*+' or ord(h) in (40, 41) for h in c
    )
    names = [
        c
        for c in dict.fromkeys(names)
        if c not in core_names
        and not (words(c) & set(core_names) and words(c) <= allowed and plain(c))
    ]
    used = list(dict.fromkeys(['redCards', 'dark_skin', 'playerShort', 'games'] + names))
    data = df.dropna(subset=used)
    finite = [c for c in used if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[c])]
    data = data[np.isfinite(data[finite].astype(float)).all(axis=1)]
    if len(data) and data['dark_skin'].nunique() < 2:
        raise ValueError('the exposure ' + 'dark_skin' + ' has the same value in every row, so it is collinear with the intercept and its effect cannot be estimated: the earlier step that builds it produced a constant. A threshold taken from a numpy median, percentile or quantile is NaN when the column has missing values, and no row then passes it. The pandas median and quantile methods skip missing values')
    core = data[['dark_skin']].astype(float)
    parts = [core]
    numeric = [c for c in names if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[c])]
    other = [c for c in names if c not in numeric]
    if numeric:
        parts.append(data[numeric].astype(float))
    if other:
        dummies = pd.get_dummies(data[other].astype(str), drop_first=True, dtype=float)
        parts.append(dummies)
    exog = sm.add_constant(pd.concat(parts, axis=1), has_constant='add')
    labels = pd.Series(exog.columns.map(str))
    repeats = labels.groupby(labels).cumcount()
    exog.columns = [f'{c}_repeat{n}' if n else c for c, n in zip(labels, repeats)]
    sources = {f'{c}_{v}': c for c in other for v in data[c].astype(str).unique()}
    target = core.iloc[:, 0].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    floor = 1e-07 * (float(np.abs(target).max()) or 1.0)
    members = {}
    for name in exog.columns:
        members.setdefault(sources.get(str(name)), []).append(name)
    for column in other:
        own = members.get(column, [])
        if not own:
            continue
        span = exog[['const', *own]].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        fitted = span @ np.linalg.lstsq(span, target, rcond=None)[0]
        if float(np.abs(target - fitted).max()) <= floor:
            exog = exog.drop(columns=own)
    protected = ['const', *map(str, core.columns)]
    basis = np.zeros((len(exog), 0))
    aliased = []
    for column in list(exog.columns):
        vector = exog[column].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        size = float(np.linalg.norm(vector))
        residual = vector / size if size else vector
        for _ in range(2):
            residual = residual - basis @ (basis.T @ residual)
        size = float(np.linalg.norm(residual))
        if size >= 1e-07:
            basis = np.column_stack([basis, residual / size])
        elif str(column) not in protected:
            aliased.append(str(column))
    kept = [c for c in exog.columns if c not in aliased]
    tangled = []
    for column in aliased:
        target = exog[column].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        weights = np.linalg.lstsq(exog[kept].to_numpy(dtype=float), target, rcond=None)[0]
        sizes = np.abs(weights) * exog[kept].abs().max().to_numpy(dtype=float)
        floor = 1e-07 * (float(np.abs(target).max()) or 1.0)
        involved = [c for c, size in zip(kept, sizes) if size > floor]
        if any(c in core.columns for c in involved):
            tangled += [c for c in involved if c not in protected]
    tangled = list(dict.fromkeys(tangled))
    exog = exog.drop(columns=aliased + tangled)
    note = 'aliased covariates dropped: ' + ', '.join(aliased) if aliased else ''
    note += '; covariates that rebuild the exposure with them dropped: ' + ', '.join(tangled) if tangled else ''
    endog = data['redCards'].astype(float)
    offset = np.log(data['games'].astype(float))
    groups = pd.factorize(data['playerShort'])[0]
    model = sm.GLM(endog, exog, family=sm.families.Poisson(), offset=offset)
    fit = model.fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": groups}, use_t=bool(len(np.unique(groups)) < 30))
    term = 'dark_skin'
    ci = fit.conf_int()
    low, high = (float(v) for v in ci.loc[term])
    value = float(fit.params[term])
    p_value = float(fit.pvalues[term])
    return {
        "estimate": float(np.exp(value)),
        "ci_low": float(np.exp(low)),
        "ci_high": float(np.exp(high)),
        "p_value": p_value,
        "n": int(len(data)),
        "note": note,
        "extra": {"coefficient": value},
    }

report.narrative: The original analysis estimated 1.08 (95% CI 0.937 to 1.24, p = 0.3, n = 116,160) and returned the verdict NO CLEAR EVIDENCE. The minimal flip changes Choose covariates for adjustment from "Position, league and referee country" to "Minimal set plus height, weight, games and referee-country bias scores". This flip changes the covariates of the model (adds games, height, meanExp, meanIAT, weight): adjusting for another set of covariates answers a different conditional question, so this is an estimand change, not a re-analysis of the same quantity. The judge accepted it because height, weight and referee-country bias scores are pre-exposure characteristics that could plausibly relate to both card rates and how raters perceive skin tone, so adjusting for them is a reasonable confounder-control choice. Under that set the estimate is 1.18 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.36, p = 0.022, n = 115,457), which reads as BIAS DETECTED. This flip was reproduced by an independent re-execution. Across the 18 explored universes, the estimate ranges from about 1.03 to 1.18. The covariate set is the choice that moves the estimate most, and the rater-averaging and model-estimator choices matter less. Several alternatives that switch the outcome measure to a Poisson rate ratio also reach BIAS DETECTED, but those are measure changes rather than pure reanalyses. The judge rejected the option of keeping only dyads with at most 20 games, and rejected trimming extreme referee-country scores, since neither had a field-based justification. Robustness: 61% of the analysis grid agrees with the original verdict and 39% reverses it.
caveats: The original analysis's model receives 124,621 of the 146,028 uploaded rows (15% left out): 'Handle players without skin-tone ratings' drops 21,407. The verdict describes the rows kept; if the dropped rows differ from them, as rows with missing values often do, it may not hold for every row.

In 6 universes the model asked statsmodels for HC1 standard errors on a Logit fit; statsmodels computes HC0 (White) standard errors for such likelihood models whatever HC variant is asked, so those intervals and p-values are HC0, not the variant the option names.

The 61% robustness estimate is the share of the analysis grid that agrees with the original verdict; it was sampled as follows: the whole grid: 18 combinations, 18 distinct results; exact, not sampled, and independent of the beam search. The universes the beam search explored are the ones closest to flipping, so their own agreement share leans toward flips and is not used as the estimate.

The minimal flip changes the covariates of the model (adds games, height, meanExp, meanIAT, weight): adjusting for another set of covariates answers a different conditional question, so this is an estimand change, not a re-analysis of the same quantity.

The option 'Poisson rate model on red-card count with games exposure, clustered by player' (estimate_red_card_model) reports a rate ratio where the original analysis reports an odds ratio: its estimates are another measure of the association, so their distance from the original estimate is partly the change of measure, not only of the analysis.
